 ## 7. Theme management
 
 Pathland theming is **application-owned over a renderer-owned token system**
 ([TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md); the wire encoding lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)
 §Design Token System). The DSL gives the author two distinct surfaces:
 
 1. **Token references in style modifiers** — semantic intent instead of a
    literal: `.foregroundStyle(Color.token("color.primary"))` emits a
    `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference the renderer resolves against the current scheme.
    No opcode is re-emitted when a token or the scheme changes.
 2. **Global theme overrides** — a batch of `STYLE::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands
    rolled at mount: a single-scheme `Theme` or an `AdaptiveTheme` light+dark
    pair (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**).
 
 > **Ownership**: the application owns theme values (base + `dark.*`) and token
 > references; the renderer owns token defaults (light + dark), effective
 > color-scheme detection, resolution (override → default → parent → fallback),
 > and interaction-state styling (hover/pressed/focus/disabled). The protocol
 > never transmits hover/click/transition styling.
 
 ### 7.1 Token-typed values
 
 Any property whose value type is `COLOR` / `F32` / `STRING` / `ENUM` MAY carry a
 **token reference** instead of a literal value (MODIFIERS.md §Value types). The
 reference rides the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) with the token path in
 the arena — **never** a packed literal. A property carries exactly one value
 (literal or reference, never both).
 
 | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL (current) | Rust DSL (current) | Emits |
 |----------------------------|--------------------|--------------------|-------|
 | `Color.token("color.primary")` | `Color.token("color.primary")` | `Color::token("color.primary")` | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref (`0x08`) in any COLOR-typed property: `COLOR` 0x100A (`.foregroundStyle`), `BACKGROUND_COLOR` 0x1001, `BORDER_COLOR` 0x1004, `SHADOW_COLOR` 0x1021, `TINT` 0x1030, … |
 | `Color.token("dark.color.surface")` | `Color.token("dark.color.surface")` | `Color::token("dark.color.surface")` | same — an explicit dark-variant reference |
 | `.padding(space.2)` / `Spacing(space.2)` | (token-valued spacing/padding) | (token-valued spacing/padding) | `DESIGN_TOKEN` ref in a F32-typed property: `PADDING` 0x1011 / `SPACING` 0x0001 / `CONTENT_MARGINS` 0x0005, … (see TOKENS.md §Generative token families) |
 
 `Color` keeps its dual identity: as a **View** it is a layout-greedy fill; as a
 token reference (`Color.token(path)`) it is a **data value** passed to
 style-taking modifiers. A token-typed property resolves renderer-side and
 **re-resolves automatically** when the effective scheme changes — overrides and
 scheme are renderer state, so no node is ever re-emitted for a theme/scheme
 change.
 
 Rules:
 
 1. Reference any token path — the standard catalog (TOKENS.md §Standard Token
    Catalog) or an application-defined path. A renderer that cannot apply a token
    falls back rather than erroring.
 2. `space.<N>` members are **generative**: reference them freely (`space.2`,
    `space.0.5`), but override only `space.base` (see §7.2 rule 2).
 3. A token reference must not be combined with a literal on the same property.
 
 ### 7.2 Global theme overrides
 
 A **theme** is a batch of token overrides. Every override defines **exactly one
 value**; combine a light and a dark `Theme` via `AdaptiveTheme` for adaptive
 theming.
 
 | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`) | Rust DSL (`pathland-view` / `pathland-engine`) | Emits |
 |----------------------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------|
 | `Theme()` — one-scheme override batch | `new Theme()` (`ThemeData`) | `Theme::new()` | one `STYLE::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` per override (`A` = arena path, `B` = valueType, `C` = value) |
 | `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `.color("color.primary", 0xFF2563EB)` | `COLOR`-typed override (sRGB `0xAARRGGBB`) |
 | `.f32("space.base", 4.0)` | `.f32("space.base", 4.0f)` | `.f32("space.base", 4.0)` | `F32`-typed override (lengths in device pixels) |
 | `.u32("…", v)` / `.u8("…", v)` | `.u32(path, int)` / `.u8(path, int)` | `.u32(path, v)` / `.u8(path, v)` | `U32` / `U8`-typed override |
 | `.string("font.body.family", "Inter")` | `.string(path, String)` | `.string(path, "Inter")` | `STRING`-typed override (arena) |
 | `AdaptiveTheme(light, dark)` | `new AdaptiveTheme(light, dark)` | `AdaptiveTheme::new(light, dark)` | light overrides as base tokens; dark overrides `dark.`-prefixed |
 
 Emission contract:
 
 - The theme is emitted **once at mount** as a frame of
   `STYLE::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` opcodes before the tree. Java: `new Emitter(sink,
   theme)` emits it at the start of the mount and `renderFull` (resync) frames;
   Rust: `Engine::apply_theme` / `Engine::apply_adaptive_theme`.
 - Overrides are **renderer state**: they never re-emit nodes and never
   participate in the diff — an unchanged tree with a theme still emits **zero**
   per-node opcodes.
 - `AdaptiveTheme` emits the light `Theme`'s overrides as base paths and the dark
   `Theme`'s with the `dark.` prefix (added automatically when the author wrote a
   bare path). The renderer derives the effective scheme from the platform and
   resolves each override against it.
 - The renderer supplies light + dark defaults for the whole Tier 1 catalog, so
   dark mode works even when the author only overrides base tokens.
 
 Authoring rules:
 
 1. Override any token in the catalog or an application-defined path; never
    assume specific renderer default values.
 2. Override `space.base` to control the whole spacing scale — individual
    `space.<N>` members MUST NOT be overridden.
 3. Overrides are **global and renderer-wide**: apply the theme once per
    session/host at mount, not per view.
 
 ---
 
 ## 8. Java DSL convergence (adopted)
 
 The Java DSL (`com.pathland.view`) has the complete surface. The convergence
 below has been **adopted** (`.of()` construction, the removal of the `View.*`
 factories, and modifiers as `ViewModifier` values); the remaining items are
 marked *optional*. The canonical contract is [§4](#4-view-surface) and
 [§5](#5-modifier-surface).
 
 | Canonical | Java (adopted) | Optional / remaining |
 |-----------|----------------|----------------------|
 | `Text("…")` | `Text.of(String)` / `Text.of(Signal<String>)` | — |
 | `Button("…", action)` / `Button(action:label:)` | `Button.of(String, Runnable)` / `Button.of(View, Runnable)` | — |
 | `Toggle("label", isOn: writable)` | `Toggle.of(String label, WritableSignal<Boolean>)` (+ `ToggleStyle` overload) | — |
 | `Slider(value: in:)` | `Slider.of(binding, min, max)` (binding first) | — |
 | `.border(color, width)` | `Border.of(Color, float)` via `.modifier(...)` | `Border.of(Color, float, float)` radius convenience |
 | `DatePicker(selection:)` | `DatePicker.of(mode, days)` | *optional* `Date`-shaped overload encoding days + millis-of-day per `SET_DATE`/`DATE_CHANGED` |
 
 Adopted conventions:
 
 - **`.of()` is the one construction path.** Every concrete view/control exposes
   a static `<ViewName>.of(...)` factory on its own class. Construction is never
   `new <ViewName>()` and never `View.<name>(...)`.
 - **The `View.*` static-factory surface is removed.** The entire factory block
   (`text`, `image`, `rectangle`, `spacer`, `vstack`, `hstack`, `zstack`,
   `button`, `textField`, `textEditor`, `toggle`, `slider`, `stepper`,
   `progressView`, `gauge`, `divider`, `grid`, `scrollView`, `lazyVStack`,
   `lazyHStack`, `lazyVGrid`, `lazyHGrid`, `picker`, `menu`, `colorPicker`,
   `datePicker`, `group`) is deleted from `View.java`.
 - **`Group` is a first-class view.** `Group.of(View...)` is a transparent
   container view (SwiftUI `Group`).
 - **Core and custom modifiers share one mechanism.** Core modifiers are
   `ViewModifier` values (`Padding.of(16)`, `ForegroundStyle.of(color)`) applied
   via `.modifier(...)` — there is **no sugar on `View`**; several modifiers at
   once use `.modifiers(...)`, innermost-first. Parameterized modifier values use
   `.of(...)`; `buttonStyle` is the `ButtonStyleMod` value.
 - **Full `ShapeKind` coverage.** `Circle.of()`, `Capsule.of()`, `Ellipse.of()`,
   `RoundedRectangle.of(cornerRadius:)`, generic `Shape.of(ShapeKind)` (for
   `Path`).
 - *Optional*: a `ButtonStyle`/`environment` path letting the trailing-action
   form (`Button(label) { action }`) read the action from the environment, if a
   Java-idiomatic trailing lambda is desirable.
 - *Optional*: a `Date`-shaped `DatePicker` binding (see table).
 - Implementation status: `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`.
 
 ---
 
 ## 9. Generation contract for a new language
 
 An AI (or a human) generating a Pathland DSL in a new language MUST produce the
 following and verify each item. This is a checklist; the authoritative details
 are the companion specs.
 
 ### 9.1 Required surface
 
 - [ ] **Views/controls** — every entry of [§4](#4-view-surface):
   `Text`, `Image`, `Color`, `Shape` (all `ShapeKind`s), `Divider`, `Spacer`,
   `ProgressView`, `Gauge`; `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `ScrollView`,
   `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`; `Button`,
   `TextField`, `SecureField`, `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`,
   `Picker`, `Menu`, `DatePicker`, `ColorPicker`.
 - [ ] **Modifiers** — every entry of [§5](#5-modifier-surface), chainable on
   any view, innermost-first, emitting one property per underlying argument.
 - [ ] **Custom modifiers / unified mechanism** — a `ViewModifier` authoring
   surface (`body(content) -> View`) + `.modifier(...)` chainable on **any**
   view; **core modifiers are implemented through the same mechanism**, never a
   separate syntax ([§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)).
 - [ ] **Signals** — `signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`,
   `get`/`set`/`update`/`asReadonly`, with equality suppression, synchronous
   flush, glitch-free propagation, error caching, write discipline, circular
   detection ([§3.1](#31-signal-surface)).
 - [ ] **Two-way bindings** — every value control takes a writable signal and
   exposes a sink the host routes its event into ([§3.2](#32-two-way-binding)).
 - [ ] **Persisted state** — `State<T>` keyed fields (or the language's
   equivalent wiring) against a platform-neutral store ([§3.3](#33-persisted-state-statet)).
 - [ ] **Gestures** — `.onTapGesture` (composed from raw pointer down/up) and
   raw `pointerEvents`/`EVENT_LISTENERS` bitmask ([§4.4](#44-gestures)).
 - [ ] **Structural reactivity (conditional rendering)** — a structural
   container over a selector signal (`Conditional.when(...)` / `Case.of` /
   `Case.otherwise`, or the language's `if`/`switch` equivalent), reconciling
   the slot into `TREE` deltas with zero opcodes for identical structure
   ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-conditional-rendering)).
 - [ ] **Navigation** — `Router` / `RouteTable` / `NavigationContainer` /
   `NavigationLink` over a plain `Signal<Route>`, the initial route host-seeded
   before mount, emitting `ROUTE` and `TRANSITION` and consuming the `NAVIGATE`
   event ([§4.5](#45-navigation)).
 - [ ] **Design tokens & theming** — a token surface: token-typed values usable
   in style modifiers (a `Color` accepting a token path, e.g. `Color.token("color.primary")`
   or the language's equivalent), a theme/override helper emitting
   `STYLE::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` (base values + `dark.`-prefixed dark values), and
   the **base=light / `dark.*`** color-scheme convention with renderer-derived
   scheme detection — see [§7](#7-theme-management) and [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md).
 
 ### 9.2 Mapping rules (signature → protocol)
 
 1. Each view/control maps to its **fixed component id** in PRIMITIVES.md.
    Application/custom component types live in `0x0100`–`0xFFFF`; a DSL must
    never reuse allocated ids.
 2. Each modifier maps to the **documented property id(s)** in MODIFIERS.md
    with the documented **value type** (U8/U32/I32/F32/STRING/ENUM/COLOR/
    DESIGN_TOKEN). Enumerated values use the numeric codes in MODIFIERS.md's
    appendix.
 3. `Color` values pack as sRGB `0xAARRGGBB`. A **token-typed** value instead
    carries the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type with the token path in the arena
    (never a packed literal); the renderer resolves it against the current
    scheme. A theme/override helper emits `STYLE::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`
    (`A` = arenaRef path, `B` = valueType, `C` = value); a `dark.`-prefixed path
    supplies the dark design (base = light — [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md)).
 4. `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` sentinels: `FILL` = −1.0, `HUG_CONTENT` = −2.0.
 5. `DatePicker` value/event use the two-field encoding **days since epoch
    (I32) + millis of day (U32)**; there is no `DATE_VALUE` property.
 6. Value/text/date events are gated by the transport-aware event guards; the
    DSL's controls emit the `ACTION_ID`/`BINDING_ID`/`EVENT_LISTENERS` that
    declare intent.
 7. Emission is **diff-based and reactive**: the DSL describes values, the
    emitter diffs. A generated DSL must keep the retained tree + emitter
    separation; it must not hand-serialize full trees.
 
 ### 9.3 Language adaptation rules
 
 | SwiftUI mechanism | Adapt as |
 |-------------------|----------|
 | trailing closure / result builder for children | varargs (Java), macros (Rust), builders/block (C#/Kotlin), element list (any) |
 | `Binding<T>` (Swift) | `WritableSignal<T>` (always — signals are the model, never property wrappers) |
 | `some View` opaque return | the language's `View` interface/trait (Java `View`, Rust `View` trait) |
 | `@State`/`@Binding` property wrappers | signals + persisted `State<T>` ([§3.3](#33-persisted-state-statet)) |
 | labeled parameters | named params where the language has them; otherwise preserve **parameter order** and document labels |
 | method chaining for modifiers | default methods (Java), extension traits (Rust), extension methods (C#/Kotlin) |
 
 ### 9.4 Conformance recipe
 
 A generated DSL is verified by proving it **emits the same bytes** as the
 reference implementations:
 
 1. Port the golden vectors in [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) into the new
    DSL's test harness; assert byte-identical `TREE`/`STYLE`/`EVENT`/`META`
    opcodes for each canonical element.
 2. Port the Java `EmitterTest` cases (mount → `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_DATE`
    deltas; unchanged tree → zero opcodes; two-way routing: `TEXT_CHANGED`,
    `VALUE_CHANGED`, `DATE_CHANGED` write into the bound signal).
 3. Verify the no-heap-allocation steady-state property where the target
    language supports it (the Rust engine proves zero dynamic allocations during
    steady-state emission).
 4. Cross-check every referenced id against PRIMITIVES.md/MODIFIERS.md/EVENTS.md
    (the specs are the source of truth, never the reference code).
 
 **Reference implementations to read**: Java — `lib/java/pathland-view`
 (`com.pathland.view`, `com.pathland.view.signal`, `com.pathland.view.state`,
 `com.pathland.view.emit`); Rust — `lib/rust/crates/pathland-view` +
 `pathland-engine` + `pathland-core::signal`.
 
 ---
 
 ## 10. Appendix A: SwiftUI ↔ DSL signature map
 
 Representative rows; the full surface is in [§4](#4-view-surface) and
 [§5](#5-modifier-surface).
 
 | SwiftUI | Canonical DSL | Java DSL (current) | Rust DSL (current) |
 |---------|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|
 | `Text("Hi")` | `Text("Hi")` | `Text.of("Hi")` | `text("Hi")` |
 | `VStack(alignment: .center, spacing: 8) { … }` | `VStack(alignment:spacing:) { … }` | `VStack.of(Alignment.CENTER, 8, children...)` | `vstack![…].modifier(Spacing.of(8.0))` |
 | `Button("+") { inc() }` | `Button("+", action)` | `Button.of("+", () -> inc())` | `button("+")` (no action yet) |
 | `TextField("Name", text: $name)` | `TextField("Name", text: writable)` | `TextField.of("Name", name)` | `TextField { placeholder }` (no binding yet) |
 | `Toggle("On", isOn: $on)` | `Toggle("On", isOn: writable)` | `Toggle.of(selected, binding)` | `Toggle(style)` (no binding yet) |
 | `Slider(value: $v, in: 0...100)` | `Slider(value: writable, in: min...max)` | `Slider.of(vSig, 0, 100)` | `Slider { value, min, max }` (no binding yet) |
 | `DatePicker("D", selection: $d)` | `DatePicker("D", selection: writable)` | `DatePicker.of(DatePickerMode.DATE, days)` | `DatePicker` (bare) |
 | `.foregroundStyle(.red)` | `.foregroundStyle(Color)` | `.modifier(ForegroundStyle.of(Color))` | `.foreground_style(Color(0xFF0000FF))` |
 | `.background(.gray)` | `.background(Color)` | `.modifier(Background.of(Color))` | `.background(Color(0xFFEEEEEE))` |
 | `.border(.blue, width: 2)` | `.border(Color, width: 2)` | `.modifier(Border.of(Color, 2))` | `.border(Color, 2.0)` |
 | `.frame(width: 100, height: 24)` | `.frame(width:height:alignment:)` | `.modifier(FrameMod.of(100, 24))` | `.frame(Some(100.0), Some(24.0), None)` |
 | `.padding(16)` | `.padding(16)` | `.modifier(Padding.of(16))` | `.padding(16.0)` |
 | `.font(.system(size: 28))` | `.font(size: 28)` | `.modifier(FontSize.of(28))` | `.font_size(28.0)` |
 | `.fontWeight(.bold)` | `.fontWeight(FontWeight)` | `.modifier(FontWeightMod.of(FontWeight.BOLD))` | `.font_weight(700.0)` |
 | `.shadow(color:radius:x:y:)` | `.shadow(color:radius:x:y:)` | `.modifier(Shadow.of(Color, float, float, float))` | (not yet) |
 | `.onTapGesture { go() }` | `.onTapGesture(action)` | `.modifier(TapGesture.of(() -> go()))` | `.on_tap_gesture(|| go())` |
 | `if showLogin { LoginView() } else { HomeView() }` | `if/else` in a result builder | `Conditional.when(showLogin, LoginView.of(), HomeView.of())` | `if`/`match` in `build()` |
 | `NavigationStack { … }` | `Router` + `NavigationContainer` | `NavigationContainer.of(router)` | `NavigationContainer::new(router)` |
 | `NavigationLink("Users", value:)` | `NavigationLink("label", router, to)` | `NavigationLink.of("Users", router, "/users")` | `navigation_link(...)` |
 | `content.modifier(Card())` | `content.modifier(Card())` | `content.modifier(CardStyle.of(...))` | `.modifier(Card)` |
 
 Core modifier sugar (`.padding`, `.foregroundStyle`, …) is shorthand for
 `.modifier(CoreModifier.of(...))` — one mechanism for built-in and
 application-authored modifiers alike ([§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)).
 The Java realization has **no sugar**: `.modifier(Padding.of(16))` is the only
 form, with `.modifiers(...)` for several at once.
 
 **Status deltas captured by this table**: the Java DSL is surface-complete —
 `<ViewName>.of(...)` construction, modifiers as values via `.modifier(...)`
 (no sugar on `View`), `ButtonStyleMod` for `.buttonStyle`; the Rust DSL is
 structural today — `pathland-view` exposes the view/modifier surface without
 signals, two-way bindings, or actions (signals live in `pathland-core::signal`
 for engine-side binding). Both are per-project implementation status tracked in
 each project's `status.md`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Conformance
 
 - The wire footprint of every DSL element above is defined by the golden
   vectors in [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md). A new DSL element MUST add
   vectors before any implementation depends on it.
 - Component ids: [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md); property ids and value
   types: [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md); event ids and listener bits:
   [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md). These specs are the single source of truth.
\ No newline at end of file

  style an active menu row or gate conditional content:
  `Signals.computed(() -> Navigation.isActive(router, path).get() ? ACTIVE : CLEAR)`.
- **The router as a scoped environment value** (SwiftUI `.environment` style):
  `Navigation.ROUTER` is an `EnvironmentKey<Router>`. A `NavigationContainer` scopes
  it to its destination subtree; any component reads
  `Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER)` during render — no constructor threading,
  nearest binding wins (nested containers override), and structural slots re-apply
  the scope when they re-render their destination.

**The active platform path is universal** — `Platform.ACTIVE_PATH` is an
`EnvironmentKey<WritableSignal<String>>` the host provides for **every** app (with
or without navigation), like SwiftUI's `onOpenURL` generalized across platforms:
```java
// host (always):
WritableSignal<String> activePath = Signals.signal(env.route());
RenderResult result = emitter.mount(
        root.environment(Platform.ACTIVE_PATH, activePath), new Environment(state));
// re-route on deep-link/popstate:
activePath.set(env.route());   // or from a NAVIGATE event URL
```
- **An app with navigation** builds a **router bound to the signal**:
  `Navigation.navigator().route(...).build(activePath)`. The signal is the source of
  truth: external writes (deep links/popstate) are re-routed **through guards** (never
  bypassed), and the router's own `navigate`/`push`/`pop`/`replace` are mirrored back
  into the signal. The initial value is guard-processed.
- **An app without navigation** just observes the signal — read it, or register
  `View.onPathChange(path -> …)` (fires on every change, including the initial value).
- `NAVIGATE` events: a URL updates `activePath` (→ bound router re-routes guard-aware,
  `onPathChange` listeners fire); a back (no URL) goes to `RenderResult.navigateHandler`
  → `router.pop()` — meaningful only when a router exists.

The `EnvironmentMod.of(key, value)` has signature `static <T> EnvironmentMod of(EnvironmentKey<T> key, T value)`. For the Signal overload, I need to pass the signal to a modifier that accepts `EnvironmentKey<T>` + `Signal<T>`. But the modifier stores a raw value (Object) into `EnvironmentValues` via `current().with(key, value)`.

Options:
1. Change `EnvironmentMod.of` to accept `(EnvironmentKey<T>, Object)` — but then the plain-value overload passes T (Object ok).
2. Add an overload `EnvironmentMod.of(EnvironmentKey<T>, Signal<T>)` that stores the signal as the raw value.

Actually the cleanest: `EnvironmentMod` stores `EnvironmentKey<Object>` + `Object value`. The value can be either a plain T or a Signal<T>. Since `EnvironmentValues.with(key, value)` stores it raw, and `Environment.value` wraps/returns signals at read, both work. So `EnvironmentMod.of` just needs to accept the value as `Object` regardless.

Let me change `EnvironmentMod.of` signature to accept `(EnvironmentKey<T>, Object)` — wait, but then the call `EnvironmentMod.of(key, value)` from the plain overload passes `T`, fine. ```java
static <T> EnvironmentMod of(EnvironmentKey<T> key, Object value) {
    return new EnvironmentMod((EnvironmentKey<Object>) key, value);
}
```

**Summary**

Reactivity today is fine-grained: a node re-emits `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY` when a signal bound to its text/property changes (`node.textBinding` / `node.propertyBindings`), and structural slots (`NavigationContainer`, `Conditional`) re-render via `Emitter.reconcileSlot` when their selector signal changes. That covers signals that a node *binds to* — but not signals a view *reads* to decide its structure.

**The gap**

A view that reads a signal inside `render()`/`body()` to pick its subtree (control flow: which branch to render, which router, which destination) is not reactive. `body()` is evaluated once at mount and never re-runs, so that read's dependency is never recorded and no structural change is ever emitted.

**Scope: ALL signals, any source**

This applies to every signal, no matter where it comes from:

- environment values (`Environment.value(key)` returns a `Signal<T>`; a bound node updates, but a `body()` read for control flow does not);
- `State` / `StateStore` signals and `PersistentState` values;
- a `Signals.signal` / `Signals.computed` captured directly by the view;
- host-provided signals (`Platform.ACTIVE_PATH`, viewport, theme, etc.).

Any node whose render depends on a signal should emit its structural changes when that signal changes.

**Mechanism (suggested)**

Generalize `Emitter.reconcileSlot`: render a subtree as a *tracked* computation so that when any signal it read during `render()`/`body()` changes, the subtree re-renders and the structural deltas are emitted.

**Constraints (non-negotiable)**

- Preserve fine-grained per-node reactivity elsewhere — an unchanged node still emits **zero** opcodes.
- Renderers stay stateless (Principle 1).
- Steady-state emission stays allocation-free.
- The diff-based emitter contract is unchanged: only actual changes are transmitted.

**Related**

- `Environment.value(key)` returns signals (feat/environment-signals).
- `spec/DSL.md` §4.5, `AGENTS.md` reactive-signals section, `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`.
EOF

- Renderers stay stateless (Principle 1).
- Steady-state emission stays allocation-free.
- The diff-based emitter contract is unchanged: only actual changes are transmitted.

- `Environment.value(key)` returns signals (feat/environment-signals).

## Why the field is null

`Environment.value(key)` doesn't return a *live channel* the environment writes into — it returns a **snapshot of the current scope's binding at call time**. The environment is a scoped, hierarchical lookup resolved during render; it never holds a reference to your field, so nothing "sets" it.

At `new Sidebar()` (inside `SplitNavDemo.body()`), the `ROUTER` scope isn't pushed yet → there's no binding to snapshot → you get a constant `() -> null`. A signal created with null *can* later be filled — but only if something writes to that exact signal, and the scope has no way to know about it.

## What your idea actually requires

For a **field** to resolve an env value, the thing it holds must be **lazy** — it must defer resolution to `.get()` (called during render, when the scope is active), not snapshot at construction. That's the `@Environment` property-wrapper trick.

So the real change is: make `Environment.value(key)` return a **lazy, scope-resolving `Signal<T>`** instead of a snapshot. Then:
```java

...

That's exactly why the current `Environment.value` **snapshots** (so the concrete binding signal is captured and stays correct in effects).

To have both, the lazy signal must **capture the binding during render and reuse it afterwards**:
- `.get()` while a scope is active → resolve the nearest binding, remember it, return its value.
- `.get()` outside render (effects) → use the remembered binding.

That needs a small "in render" marker (e.g. a depth counter bumped by `EnvironmentView` / `NavigationContainer` / `reconcileSlot`), plus per-signal captured state. Edge cases to define: a view instance reused across two scopes; a scope that deliberately binds `null` vs. no scope at all (capture-on-found vs. capture-always).

2. **Constructor injection** — `new Sidebar(router)`, plain Java, no env.
3. **Reintroduce a lazy proxy** (`Environment.ref(key)`) — field-friendly; it's the one extra thing you removed.

Let me also double-check `PathChangeView`: `node.activePath = Environment.value(Platform.ACTIVE_PATH);` — during render, ACTIVE_PATH bound → concrete WritableSignal (typed as Signal<String> now). ✓. The emitter's effect reads it → works. ✓.

OK, I think the design is solid. Let me write the plan.

Also, I should consider: does the hybrid change `Environment.value`'s behavior for the existing `environmentValueReturnsSignal` test's `assertSame(host, sigSeen.get(0))`? The probe render reads during a bound scope → concrete host → assertSame passes. ✓.

Now, let me also decide the class name and location: `EnvironmentSignal<T>` (package-private) in `com.pathland.view`, or a nested class. Since it's internal, package-private top-level `EnvironmentSignal.java` or nested in `Environment`. Given we just consolidated, a nested private static class inside `Environment` is cleanest (no new public type). Let me plan a package-private static nested class in `Environment` or a separate package-private file. Nested private static class in `Environment` is fine (it's an implementation detail). But it implements `Signal<T>` and needs `toSignal` helper. Fine.

Let me now write the plan. Structure:

Also note: with the hybrid, if the key is bound at field-creation time, the field holds the concrete signal (snapshot) — and won't re-resolve if the scope later changes. But that's the current behavior for bindings anyway. The lazy path is for the not-yet-bound case.

parts.text: Tell me about The alternative- a fully uniform wrapper

The user wants me to explain the alternative — a fully uniform wrapper — versus the hybrid. I'm in plan mode (read-only). Let me explain the design, its consequences, and the tradeoffs, and how the Router would need to change.

Let me think through the fully uniform wrapper design carefully.

**Fully uniform wrapper:**
`Environment.value(key)` ALWAYS returns a lazy `EnvironmentSignal<T>` wrapper (no snapshot-when-bound branch). The wrapper resolves the current scope on `.get()`:
- If the key is bound in the current scope → capture the binding (nearest wins), delegate.
- Else → use the last captured binding (or null).

This is conceptually cleaner: one code path, one return type, no asymmetry. The returned object is always an `EnvironmentSignal` (a lazy proxy), never the concrete binding.

**Consequences:**

1. **Identity/instanceof**: The wrapper is NOT the concrete binding. So:
   - `assertSame(host, Environment.value(sigKey))` would FAIL (returns the wrapper, not `host`). The test would change to check `.get()` equality or a way to unwrap.
   - `Router`'s `activePath instanceof WritableSignal<String>` would be FALSE → `boundPath = null` → navigation mirroring breaks.

2. **Node bindings**: The wrapper delegates `.get()` to the captured binding. During render, `Environment.value(key)` returns the wrapper; the emitter stores the wrapper as `textBinding`; the effect calls wrapper `.get()`. Outside render, the wrapper uses the captured binding. For this to work, the wrapper must have captured the binding during render. But `Environment.value(key)` is called during render (key bound) → the wrapper could capture eagerly in its constructor. So the wrapper, if constructed when the key is bound, pre-captures. That works for node bindings. But if constructed when NOT bound (field case), it captures on first scoped `.get()`.

   Wait — so even in the uniform design, the wrapper would want to eagerly capture at construction when bound (otherwise node bindings break, since their `.get()` is outside render). So the uniform wrapper still needs an "eager capture if bound at construction" step. That's basically the same `contains` check — just always wrapped instead of returning concrete. So uniform = always wrap, but pre-capture when bound.

3. **Reactivity/tracking**: The wrapper delegates `.get()` to the captured binding signal. If the binding is a Signal, reading the wrapper tracks the underlying signal (because the wrapper's `.get()` calls `captured.get()`, which registers the dependency in the current reactive context). ✓ So tracking works.

4. **Router write access**: This is the crux. The Router needs a `WritableSignal<String>` to mirror navigation. With the uniform wrapper, `Environment.value(ACTIVE_PATH)` returns `EnvironmentSignal<String>` (a read-only `Signal`). The Router can't `set()` it.

   Options to fix:
   a. **Wrapper implements `WritableSignal`** and delegates writes to the captured binding if it's writable (throws otherwise). Then `instanceof WritableSignal` is true, and `boundPath.set(path)` delegates to the host's writable. But: the wrapper is typed `Signal<T>` by `Environment.value`; at runtime it's a `WritableSignal`. The Router's instanceof passes. `set()` delegates if the captured binding is writable. This works but is "surprising" — a signal that's secretly writable, and `set()` throws for non-writable bindings.
      - Also: the wrapper must have captured the binding before `set()` is called. Since the Router captures at construction (during render, ACTIVE_PATH bound), the wrapper pre-captures → writable known. ✓
   b. **Expose the concrete binding**: add a method to unwrap, e.g. `Environment.resolve(signal)` or the wrapper exposes `binding()`. The Router calls `Environment.writable(activePath)` or similar to get the underlying `WritableSignal` (or null). This reintroduces an accessor but at the Router level, not app level.
   c. **Change Router to not need a writable**: e.g., the Router writes back via a callback/event that the host applies. Bigger architectural change.

   Option (a) is the most "uniform" and keeps the Router unchanged, but adds a delegating-writable wrapper (more machinery + surprising semantics). Option (b) is explicit but adds an unwrap API.

5. **`instanceof` generally**: Any app code doing `instanceof` on an env read would break. Currently only the Router does. With (a), it works. With (b), the Router unwraps.

6. **Scoping/dynamism**: The uniform wrapper is *more* dynamic — every `.get()` re-resolves the current scope (if bound). This is more correct for scope changes but also more "ambient" (the value depends on when `.get()` is called). The hybrid returns a concrete snapshot when bound, so it's less dynamic. For a field read in `body()`, both work. For a field whose `.get()` is called in different scopes, the uniform wrapper re-resolves (nearest wins each time) — arguably better.

7. **Memory/alloc**: Uniform creates a wrapper object per `Environment.value` call; hybrid creates a wrapper only when unbound. Minor.

8. **Equality of EnvironmentValues**: unaffected (stores raw values).

9. **`contains` still needed** for the wrapper's resolution.

10. **Tests**: 
    - `assertSame(host, ...)` → changes (uniform returns wrapper). Could assert `wrapper.get()` equals, and if the wrapper delegates, `wrapper.get() == host.get()`. Or test that writing to the wrapper delegates.
    - A "delegating writable" test: `((WritableSignal) Environment.value(ACTIVE_PATH)).set("/x")` updates the host signal.

Let me also think about a subtlety with the uniform wrapper + delegating writable + the Router:
- `Router(RouteTable, Signal<String> activePath)`: `activePath instanceof WritableSignal<String>` → true (wrapper implements WritableSignal). `boundPath = wrapper`. Then `boundPath.set(path)` → wrapper.set → delegates to the host writable. And `boundPath.get()` → wrapper.get → captured binding (host writable).get(). ✓
- But the wrapper implements WritableSignal even when the binding is a plain value or null (non-writable). Then `set()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`/`IllegalStateException`. The Router only calls set when it decided to bind (instanceof true) — but instanceof is ALWAYS true for the wrapper, even when the binding is a plain value! So the Router would bind `boundPath = wrapper` even for a non-writable binding, and later `set()` would throw. That's a bug: the Router's "mirror only when writable" logic breaks because the wrapper always claims to be WritableSignal.

   To fix, the Router would need a different check: e.g., `Environment.isWritable(activePath)` or `activePath` exposes writability. Or the wrapper's `instanceof WritableSignal` is only true when the binding is writable — impossible (type is static). So the "delegating writable wrapper" forces the Router to use a new capability check rather than `instanceof`.

   So option (a) requires changing the Router's writability check anyway (can't use instanceof). E.g., add `Environment.writable(signal)` returning `Optional<WritableSignal>` or null. That's option (b)-ish.

   Hmm. So the uniform approach inevitably needs a new capability API for the Router (either `Environment.writable(...)` or a wrapper method). Because a wrapper can't conditionally be a WritableSignal.

Let me reconsider: Could the wrapper be created as a `WritableSignal` only when the binding is writable? `Environment.value` returns `Signal<T>`; it could return a `WritableEnvironmentSignal` (implements WritableSignal) when the bound value is writable, and a plain `EnvironmentSignal` otherwise. Then `instanceof WritableSignal` is true only for writable bindings. ✓ That preserves the Router's check!
- But "bound value is writable" is only known when the wrapper resolves the binding. If the wrapper is created when bound (pre-captured), it knows. If created when unbound (field), it doesn't know yet → can't choose the type. For ACTIVE_PATH, the app reads it when bound → could return the writable wrapper. For the field case (ROUTER, plain), returns plain wrapper. Hmm, this works for the ACTIVE_PATH read (bound at read). So `Environment.value` could:
  - If bound: binding = scope.get(key); if binding is WritableSignal → return a WritableEnvironmentSignal wrapper; if Signal → return a plain delegating wrapper; if plain → return a constant.
  - If not bound: return a lazy plain wrapper.
  
  But that's basically the hybrid again (special-casing when bound), just always wrapped. And the "writable wrapper" still needs to delegate `set()`.

Honestly, the uniform wrapper doesn't remove complexity — it relocates it into the wrapper (delegation, writability) and still needs a capability check for the Router.

Let me now also consider: is the uniform wrapper's "always delegating" behavior actually simpler than the hybrid? The hybrid returns the concrete signal when bound (zero wrapper) and a wrapper when unbound. The uniform always wraps. The uniform is "one type always," but that type is more complex (delegation + optional writability).

Let me also think about a **fully uniform, read-only** wrapper (no writability): `Environment.value` always returns a lazy `Signal<T>` wrapper. The Router can't write → we change the Router to get write access differently. This is the cleanest conceptually but requires the biggest Router change.

Router change options for the read-only-uniform:
- The host injects the writable ACTIVE_PATH; the app reads a read-only signal for binding/reading; for the Router's mirror, the Router needs the writable. Could the Router instead not mirror directly, but emit a "route change" that the host applies? On the web, the DOM client already mirrors the route to the URL (pushState). On desktop (GTK), the router navigates internally. The mirror into ACTIVE_PATH is for the host to know the current path. Hmm.
- Or: expose `Environment.writable(key)` returning the underlying `WritableSignal` (or null). Then SplitNavDemo: `.build(Environment.writable(Platform.ACTIVE_PATH))`. But that's the accessor the user rejected earlier ("writes via the environment modifier"). Hmm — actually the user rejected `Environment.writable` because they wanted writes via the modifier. But then we changed `Router.build(Signal<String>)` + instanceof. With a uniform read-only wrapper, instanceof fails, so we'd need `Environment.writable` after all — which the user didn't want.

So the uniform read-only wrapper conflicts with the user's earlier Q2 preference (no writable accessor).

**Summary of the alternative (uniform wrapper):**
- Conceptually cleaner: `Environment.value` always returns one lazy proxy type; no snapshot/lazy asymmetry.
- But it moves complexity into the wrapper and breaks two things:
  1. `instanceof WritableSignal` (Router) — a proxy can't conditionally be writable; needs either a delegating-writable wrapper (with a separate writability check) or an unwrap/`Environment.writable` accessor (which you rejected).
  2. Instance identity — `assertSame(host, ...)` fails; tests and any identity-based logic change.
- It also makes reads *more ambient* (re-resolve on every `.get()`), which is arguably more correct for scope changes but means a signal's value depends on when it's read.
- Extra wrapper allocation per read.

**Why the hybrid is recommended:**
- Reads that happen during render when the key is bound (the common case: node bindings, `ACTIVE_PATH` for the Router) get the concrete signal → identity, `instanceof WritableSignal`, and reactivity all preserved with zero new machinery.
- Only the not-yet-bound field case gets a lazy wrapper → exactly the new capability we need.
- Net: smallest change, preserves all existing semantics, adds the field style.

Let me also mention: there's a subtle behavioral difference — the hybrid's bound-case snapshot doesn't re-resolve if the scope changes without a re-render; the uniform wrapper would. In practice, scope changes come with re-renders (structural slots), so it's moot.

Now, I should present this clearly and concisely. The user asked "Tell me about The alternative - a fully uniform wrapper." So explain it, its tradeoffs, and why the hybrid is recommended. Then ask if they still want the hybrid (or the alternative).

Let me structure:
1. What it is.
2. How it works (always wrap, delegate, capture).
3. What breaks / what it costs:
   - Router writability (the big one) — two sub-options.
   - Identity/assertSame.
   - More ambient reads.
   - Extra allocation.
4. Comparison table (hybrid vs uniform).
5. Recommendation.

I must not edit anything. Just explain and ask.

Let me write it.

Let me be careful about accuracy re: the Router. Current Router code: `this.boundPath = activePath instanceof WritableSignal<String> ws ? ws : null;`. With a uniform wrapper that always implements `Signal` (not WritableSignal), instanceof is false → boundPath null → no mirror. With a wrapper that implements WritableSignal always → instanceof true even for non-writable → set() would need to throw; Router would try to mirror and throw at runtime for non-writable bindings. So neither works cleanly without a capability check.

Also note: the wrapper could expose whether it's writable via a method, but then the Router needs to know the wrapper type → coupling.

Let me write the response.
Would the uniform be the better design?

The user asks: "Would the uniform be the better design?" This is a design judgment question. I'm in plan mode, read-only. I should give my honest assessment.

Let me think carefully about which is genuinely better, not just "less disruptive."

Let me reason about the architecture principles:
- Pathland values: protocol-first, declarative, fine-grained reactivity, zero-alloc steady state, stateless renderers.
- The environment is a scoped, hierarchical value store resolved during render.

Key considerations for "better design":

1. **Conceptual clarity**: The uniform wrapper has one mental model: "an env read is a lazy proxy that resolves the current scope." The hybrid has two behaviors depending on timing — which is a subtle leak of implementation into semantics. A reader of `Environment.value(key)` can't tell from the type whether they got a concrete signal or a lazy proxy. That asymmetry can surprise: e.g., the returned signal's identity differs; whether it re-resolves on scope change differs. So uniform is more predictable in its *type* and *behavior* contract.

2. **Correctness of scoping/dynamism**: The uniform wrapper re-resolves the current scope on every `.get()`. This is arguably more correct: if a scope changes (e.g., a structural slot re-renders with a new router), reads reflect it. The hybrid snapshots when bound, so a bound read is fixed at read time. In practice scope changes come with re-renders, so the hybrid is fine. But uniform is more robust.

3. **The Router / writability**: This is the real cost. The uniform wrapper needs a capability API. But is that actually a *worse* design? Arguably a capability API (`Environment.writable(key)` or an unwrap) is *more honest* than relying on `instanceof` on a signal returned by a read. `instanceof WritableSignal` is itself a bit of a smell — it's runtime type introspection to discover a capability. A dedicated accessor/contract is arguably cleaner. So the uniform design's need for a capability API might actually improve the design, not degrade it.

   But: the user earlier rejected `Environment.writable` (Q2) in favor of "writes via the environment modifier." So introducing a capability API reopens that. However, we could design it differently: the wrapper could expose its resolved binding, or the Router could accept a `Signal<String>` and get write access via a well-defined "writable env binding" concept.

   Actually — reconsider: what if the environment value for ACTIVE_PATH is *typed* as a `WritableSignal`? I.e., the key is `EnvironmentKey<WritableSignal<String>>`... no, we changed away from that. Hmm.

   Alternative: keep the hybrid specifically for the Router by having `Environment.value` return the concrete binding when bound. That's the hybrid.

4. **Allocation**: uniform allocates a wrapper per read. In steady-state emission, env reads happen at render (mount) and in structural re-renders. Not in the hot delta path. So allocation is not a real concern. (AGENTS.md zero-alloc is about steady-state *emission*, not render.) So this cost is negligible.

5. **Node bindings**: With uniform + eager capture-if-bound at construction, node bindings work (wrapper delegates). So no regression there, provided the wrapper pre-captures when bound. Actually, do we need eager capture? If the wrapper's first `.get()` is outside render (emitter effect) and the wrapper didn't capture at construction (because... it was constructed during render while bound → captureIfBound at construction captures). So yes, constructor capture handles it. If constructed unbound and only read by the emitter → the documented limitation (same as hybrid). So uniform has the SAME limitation.

6. **Identity**: uniform loses `assertSame`. But do we rely on identity? The test does. We can change it. Identity of env signals isn't a documented contract. So minor.

7. **Ambient reads**: uniform's "value depends on when you read" is a double-edged sword. For `@Environment`, that's the intended semantics (resolve current scope). SwiftUI's `@Environment` reads at body-eval time. So ambient-during-render is the norm. The uniform wrapper matches SwiftUI better.

So on pure design merit, the uniform wrapper is arguably **more principled**:
- One type, one behavior contract.
- Matches the `@Environment` mental model (resolve at read).
- Removes the `instanceof WritableSignal` smell in favor of an explicit capability.
- More robust to scope changes.

The hybrid is **more pragmatic/minimal**:
- Preserves all current semantics and tests.
- No new capability API.
- But has a subtle timing-dependent asymmetry.

Which is "better"? It depends on what we optimize for. If this is a foundational API (the environment mechanism), I'd lean toward the uniform wrapper being the better *long-term* design, because:
- The hybrid's asymmetry is the kind of subtlety that causes bugs later (someone returns a concrete signal vs a proxy and code behaves differently).
- `instanceof WritableSignal` is a code smell; an explicit capability is cleaner.
- The environment is central enough that a clean, uniform contract pays off.

BUT the uniform design requires resolving the Router's write-access API, which reopens the Q2 decision. And the user's Q2 preference ("writes via the environment modifier") suggests they want the modifier to be the write surface. With uniform, the Router needs the writable — so either:
- `Environment.writable(key)` (an accessor) — conflicts with Q2 preference.
- Or the Router obtains the writable via the wrapper exposing it — still an accessor-ish.
- Or restructure so the Router doesn't write directly (e.g., navigation intents flow to the host, which owns the signal). That's a bigger but arguably cleaner design: the host owns ACTIVE_PATH; the Router emits navigation; the host applies it. But the Router currently mirrors to keep the host in sync.

Hmm. Let me think about whether the uniform wrapper can preserve the Router without a new public accessor.

Idea: The uniform wrapper could implement `WritableSignal<T>` and delegate `set()` to the captured binding *if writable*, and throw if not. The Router's `instanceof WritableSignal` would then always be true → it would always bind → and `set()` would throw for non-writable bindings. Unless the Router checks writability differently.

Could the wrapper expose `boolean writable()` and the Router check that? That's a capability method on the wrapper type — but the Router receives `Signal<String>`, not the wrapper type. Unless the wrapper is public or there's an interface. E.g., define an interface `EnvironmentBinding<T> extends Signal<T> { Optional<WritableSignal<T>> writable(); }` — the Router checks `instanceof EnvironmentBinding`. That's a cleaner capability contract than `instanceof WritableSignal`. And the app still just calls `Environment.value(ACTIVE_PATH)`.

So the uniform design could introduce a small interface (e.g., `EnvironmentSignal` or a `Writable`-capability) that the Router uses. That's arguably cleaner than the current `instanceof WritableSignal` and doesn't add a public accessor to `Environment`.

But it does add a public-ish type. Hmm.

Alternatively: since the environment scope stores the raw binding, and `Environment.value` returns a wrapper, we could keep the Router's `instanceof WritableSignal` working by having `Environment.value` return the *concrete* signal when bound... that's the hybrid again.

OK so the real question: is the uniform wrapper's cleanliness worth (a) a capability interface/API for the Router, and (b) the identity change?

My honest assessment: 
- For a *foundational* mechanism like environment, uniformity and a single, predictable contract is better long-term. The hybrid's asymmetry is a design smell that will bite.
- But the uniform wrapper's benefit is mostly conceptual; the practical behavior for current use cases is nearly identical.
- The deciding factor is the Router/writability API: if we can define a clean capability (e.g., the env signal exposes its resolved binding, or a `WritableSignal` view), uniform is better. If we'd have to add an ugly accessor or hack, hybrid wins.

Let me also consider a middle path: **uniform wrapper, but the Router receives the env binding's concrete writable via a well-defined unwrap.** E.g., `Environment.value(ACTIVE_PATH)` returns the wrapper; `Router.build(Signal<String>)`; inside, the Router does `activePath instanceof WritableSignal` OR the wrapper implements a method. Hmm.

Actually — here's a cleaner uniform design that sidesteps the whole issue: **make the wrapper transparent for capability by having `Environment.value` return a signal that delegates, and give the Router a dedicated "bind to platform path" API that reads the environment itself.** But that couples Router to Environment.

Hmm, let me think about the actual best design holistically:

The cleanest conceptual model:
- `Environment.value(key)` → a `Signal<T>` proxy that resolves the current scope lazily. (Uniform.)
- For write access (the router mirror), the environment exposes the binding as a `WritableSignal` when the injected value is writable — via the same proxy if it implements a capability, OR via a separate typed read.

Actually, maybe the cleanest: the env value for ACTIVE_PATH is conceptually a *writable binding*. Instead of `EnvironmentKey<String>`, use `EnvironmentKey<WritableSignal<String>>`? No — that returns the signal, not the value.

Hmm, let me reconsider the whole ACTIVE_PATH typing. What if the key is `EnvironmentKey<String>` and there's a `Environment.writable(key)` returning `WritableSignal<String>`? The user rejected this. But maybe the user's rejection was about avoiding *two accessors for reading*; `writable` is a write-capability accessor, which is different. Actually the user said "I would prefer that writes are done via the environment modifier for now. Does that cover it?" and I said yes (via Router.build(Signal) + instanceof). So the user is fine with the current approach.

So introducing `Environment.writable` would contradict that. The hybrid preserves the current approach.

Let me weigh honestly:
- If we value minimal disruption and preserving the just-settled Router design: hybrid.
- If we value a single predictable contract: uniform, at the cost of reopening the Router write API.

I think the honest answer is: **the uniform wrapper is the more principled design, but its advantage is mostly conceptual and it reopens the Router writability question; the hybrid is the pragmatic choice that preserves current semantics.** Whether uniform is "better" depends on whether you're willing to redesign the Router's write access.

Actually, let me reconsider whether uniform really needs a new Router API, or whether the wrapper can be designed so `instanceof WritableSignal` works correctly.

The problem: `instanceof WritableSignal` must be true iff the binding is writable. The wrapper type is static. So it can't vary. UNLESS `Environment.value` returns different wrapper types based on the binding:
- If the bound binding is a WritableSignal → return a `WritableEnvSignal` (implements WritableSignal, delegates).
- If bound binding is a Signal → return `EnvSignal`.
- If bound binding is plain → constant.
- If unbound → lazy `EnvSignal`.

But that's branching on bound-ness again — i.e., it's the hybrid with wrappers instead of returning the concrete signal. The only difference from the hybrid is that bound reads return a *wrapper* instead of the concrete signal. That adds no value over the hybrid (it just wraps the concrete signal for no reason). So the "pure uniform" (always one type) can't preserve `instanceof WritableSignal`.

Therefore: uniform → new Router capability API. That's the tradeoff.

So, my answer: 
- Uniform is conceptually cleaner (one contract, matches @Environment, no timing asymmetry, removes instanceof smell).
- But it requires a Router write-capability API (or a delegating wrapper + capability check), and it changes identity semantics.
- The hybrid is pragmatic and preserves everything, at the cost of a subtle asymmetry.

For Pathland specifically, given it's a young protocol/framework and the environment API is foundational, I'd lean slightly toward uniform being the better *long-term* design — IF we're willing to define a clean capability contract. But the current Router approach (`instanceof WritableSignal`) is itself a smell that uniform would force us to fix properly.

Hmm, but actually — is `instanceof WritableSignal` a smell? It's a runtime capability check on the host-provided signal. In a signal system, `WritableSignal extends Signal`, so checking writability via instanceof is a reasonable idiom. Not a terrible smell.

Honest answer: **no — for this codebase the hybrid is the better design.** Uniform has real conceptual appeal, but its advantages don't outweigh what it costs here. Here's the reasoning.

## The two designs differ in exactly one place

The lazy wrapper class is **identical** in both. The only difference is what `Environment.value(key)` returns when the key **is** bound:

- **Hybrid:** the concrete binding (the injected `WritableSignal`, or a constant for a plain value).
- **Uniform:** the wrapper anyway (pre-captured).

So "uniform" isn't a different mechanism — it's the choice to route bound reads through a proxy *even when the real signal is right there*.

## Why that makes the hybrid better

1. **Uniform discards information for no gain.** When bound, the hybrid hands back the actual signal — same identity, same `WritableSignal` capability, direct reactivity. Uniform replaces that with a proxy that does the same `.get()` but *loses* identity and capability. You pay complexity and lose fidelity; behavior is otherwise identical.

2. **It forces a Router redesign (reopens Q2).** Because a proxy can't conditionally be a `WritableSignal`, uniform breaks `activePath instanceof WritableSignal` → either you add `Environment.writable(...)` (the accessor you rejected) or a delegating-writable wrapper plus a separate writability check. The hybrid preserves the `Router` exactly as you settled it.

3. **"Always ambient" isn't strictly better — it's differently surprising.** Uniform re-resolves the current scope on every `.get()`. That's closer to SwiftUI during render, but reads that happen *outside* render (the emitter's binding effects) fall back to the last capture anyway — so it's only "ambient" half the time, which is its own asymmetry.

4. **The contract is already uniform where it matters.** Both return `Signal<T>` meaning "the scoped value." The only observable difference is identity/capability — and on that axis the hybrid is strictly *more* capable.

The single genuine merit of uniform — one always-a-proxy rule — is a purity win, not a functional one. And its cost (Router write-access rework, identity changes, no concrete binding) is concrete.

## When uniform *would* be better

If we later want every env read to be a stable, re-resolving handle (e.g., a signal whose value tracks scope changes across re-renders without re-reading), uniform becomes the right call — and at that point the `WritableSignal` capability should become an explicit contract (e.g., a `WritableEnvironmentBinding` interface the `Router` checks) rather than `instanceof`. That's a coherent future direction, but it's a bigger change than what you asked for.

## Recommendation

Go with the **hybrid** now: it preserves every current semantic (node bindings, `Router` mirroring, identity), adds the field style you want, and is the smallest, least surprising change. If you want, I can note the uniform wrapper as a possible future refactor in the issue/status docs.

Shall I proceed with the hybrid as planned?

 # Pathland DSL Authoring Contract
 
 **Wire protocol version:** 1
 **Status:** Draft
 **Last Updated:** September 3, 2026
 
 ---
 
 ## Purpose
 
 This document defines the **authoring surface** — the SwiftUI-shaped DSL an
 application developer writes — for every Pathland implementation. Where
 [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md), [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md), and
 [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) describe the **wire surface** (component types,
 property ids, events, opcodes), this file describes the **surface in source
 code**: how views, controls, modifiers, and state are *named*, *ordered*, and
 *composed* so that any language can expose a conformant, idiomatic DSL.
 
 A DSL in a new language is **conformant** when it:
 
 1. exposes the full surface catalogued here (views, controls, modifiers,
    signals, state);
 2. maps every DSL element to the exact protocol component/property/event
    documented in the companion specs (no re-interpretation, no reallocation);
 3. produces **byte-identical opcode output** for the same source tree as the
    reference implementations (see the [Generation
    contract](#9-generation-contract-for-a-new-language)).
 
 ### Relationship to the other specs
 
 | File | Role |
 |------|------|
 | [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md) | Wire format: categories, commands, 16-byte opcode layout, ring/arena, value types |
 | [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md) | Which **views/nodes** exist and their component ids |
 | [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md) | Which **modifiers** (properties) exist and how they encode |
 | [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) | Which **core events** (raw inputs) exist and how they encode |
 | [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) | Golden byte vectors |
 | [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md) | Design-token catalog, resolution, and color-scheme contract |
 | **DSL.md** (this file) | How an application **author** composes those into source code |
 
 > **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
 > in each protocol crate/library), **not** in this specification. The Java DSL
 > (`com.pathland.view`) and the Rust DSL (`pathland-view`) are the two reference
 > realizations and are cited here by their **current signatures**; where they
 > diverge from the canonical form below, that divergence is noted as a *delta*,
 > and [§8](#8-java-dsl-convergence-adopted) records the adopted Java convergence.
 > This document defines the contract only.
 
 ### Two guiding rules
 
 1. **Stay as close to SwiftUI as possible.** View names, modifier names, and
    signature shapes mirror SwiftUI. Adapt only where the host language forces
    it (Rust snake_case + macros; Java camelCase + static factories), and never
    in a way that reorders or renames the canonical parameters.
 2. **State variables are signals.** Pathland does **not** use SwiftUI's
    `@State`/`@Binding` property wrappers. The view syntax is SwiftUI; the
    reactivity model is Angular-style signals (writable signals, computeds,
    effects, two-way bindings). A generated DSL MUST expose the signal surface
    of [§3](#3-state-model-signals).
 
 ---
 
 ## 1. Design principles (DSL-flavored)
 
 These recap the protocol's non-negotiables in author-facing terms. A conformant
 DSL must be *shaped* by them:
 
 - **Declarative structure, never positions.** The DSL expresses `WHAT` — a
   `VStack`, a `HStack`, a `Text` — and constraint properties (spacing, padding,
   alignment, size hints). It never computes bounds and never emits rects.
 - **`body()` is evaluated once at mount.** A composite view declares its
   subtree once; reactivity comes from **signals**, never from re-evaluating the
   body. This is what lets the emitter produce fine-grained
   `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_DATE` deltas instead of rebuilding the tree.
   The one sanctioned exception is a **structural container**
   ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-conditional-rendering)): its content is
   re-evaluated on a signal change and the emitter reconciles the retained
   subtree into `TREE` deltas.
 - **Modifiers are decoupled from views — and never hard-bound to a view
   type.** Any modifier applies to any view (`.padding` works on a `Text` and a
   `VStack` alike), and any developer can **author a custom modifier in
   application code** (a `ViewModifier`) that applies to any existing view —
   library primitive, container, control, custom view, or an already-modified
   view (see [§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)). A modifier a
   given renderer cannot apply is **allowed and ignored** — the property is
   still emitted.
 - **There is exactly one modifier mechanism.** Built-in core modifiers are
   **not** a separate syntax: they are `ViewModifier` values the library ships,
   and the sugar methods (`.padding(_:)`, `.foregroundStyle(_:)`) are
   conveniences that construct them via `.modifier(...)`. Core and
   application-authored modifiers share the same surface.
 - **Constructor properties vs modifiers.** Structural/layout parameters
   (`alignment`, `spacing`) are **constructor arguments**, never chainable.
   Everything decorative (padding, color, font, frame, border, …) is a
   **chainable modifier**. There is no standalone width/height — use the
   compound `frame` modifier.
 - **`Color` is never a modifier.** `Color` has SwiftUI's dual identity: it is a
   **View** (a layout-greedy solid-color fill) and a **Data Type** (passed into
   style-taking modifiers: `.foregroundStyle`, `.background`, `.border`,
   `.tint`). There is **no** `.color()` modifier, and `.foregroundColor(_:)` is
   deprecated — foreground styling is always `.foregroundStyle(_:)`.
 - **Only changes are transmitted.** Emission is diff-based; an unchanged tree
   emits **zero** opcodes. The DSL describes values; the emitter diffs them.
 - **Typed enums, never raw ints.** Every enumerated value is a typed constant
   (`Alignment.leading`, `FontWeight.bold`, `ToggleStyle.checkbox`), not a bare
   integer. The numeric code is the DSL's job to resolve (see the value-type and
   enum tables in MODIFIERS.md).

 ## 2. Canonical signature notation
 
 The canonical signatures below are written SwiftUI-shaped and language
 agnostic. Conventions used:
 
 - `T("…")` / `View("…")` — a view/control constructor.
 - `{ ... }` — the child subtree (a trailing closure in SwiftUI; a vararg,
   macro, builder, or lambda in other languages).
 - `Signal<T>` — a read-only derived or writable signal; `WritableSignal<T>` —
   a two-way binding target. A control takes a `WritableSignal<T>` for its
   value (see [§3](#3-state-model-signals)).
 - `()` — the action a `Button` fires.
 - `.modifier(name)` — apply a **modifier value** to a view; chainable on any
   view. Every modifier — built-in or application-authored — is such a value
   ([§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)); the sugar names
   (`.padding`, `.foregroundStyle`, …) are shorthand that construct the
   built-in values.
 - Modifiers chain as `.name(args)` on any view and are applied
   **innermost-first** (the last chained modifier's property wins).
 
 Per-language adaptation rules:
 
 | Language | Case | Composition mechanism | Example |
 |----------|------|-----------------------|---------|
 | SwiftUI | `camelCase` | trailing closures + result builder | `VStack { Text("x").padding() }` |
 | Java (`com.pathland.view`) | `camelCase` | `.of()` factories + varargs + `.modifier(...)`/`.modifiers(...)` | `VStack.of(Text.of("x").modifier(Padding.of(16)))` |
 | Rust (`pathland-view`) | `snake_case` | macros + free functions + chainable trait methods | `vstack![text("x").padding(16.0)]` |

 ## 3. State model (signals)
 
 Pathland state is **Angular-style signals**. This is the non-negotiable
 reactive core every DSL exposes.
 
 ### 3.1 Signal surface
 
 | Canonical | Java DSL (`com.pathland.view.signal`) | Semantics |
 |-----------|--------------------------------------|-----------|
 | `signal(initial)` | `Signals.signal(T)` | a writable signal |
 | `signal(name, initial)` | `Signals.signal(String, T)` | named (names surface in dependency errors) |
 | `signal(initial, equal)` | `Signals.signal(T, BiPredicate<T,T>)` | custom equality |
 | `computed(fn)` | `Signals.computed(Supplier<T>)` | lazy, memoized derived signal |
 | `effect(fn)` | `Signals.effect(Runnable)` | runs immediately, then on dependency change |
 | `untracked(fn)` | `Signals.untracked(Supplier<T>)` | reads without recording dependencies |
 | `read()` | `get()` | current value |
 | `write(v)` | `set(T)` | replace (no-op when equal) |
 | `update(fn)` | `update(UnaryOperator<T>)` | derive from current and write |
 | `asReadonly()` | `asReadonly()` | read-only view of a writable signal |
 
 **Guarantees** (must be preserved by any implementation): equality suppression,
 synchronous flush at the end of the outermost write, glitch-free propagation
 (each computed recomputes at most once per flush), error caching, write
 discipline, and circular-dependency detection.
 
 ### 3.2 Two-way binding
 
 A control's value is **a `WritableSignal<T>` passed to its constructor**:
 `TextField(placeholder, writable)`, `Toggle(label, isOn: writable)`,
 `Slider(value: writable, in: min...max)`. The flow:
 
 1. At **mount**, the DSL control records a **value input** (a sink on the
    retained node) for the signal, and the emitter exposes routing registries to
    the host: tap actions, text inputs, value inputs, date inputs.
 2. The host receives the control's raw event (`TEXT_CHANGED`,
    `VALUE_CHANGED`, `DATE_CHANGED`, or a composed tap) and calls the sink,
    which **writes into the signal**.
 3. The signal flush re-emits **only that node's** delta (`SET_TEXT`,
    `SET_PROPERTY`, `SET_DATE`) back through the emitter.
 
 Reading is equally fine-grained: a node's text or a property can be **bound to
 a signal** (`Text(signal)`, `.foregroundStyle(signal)`, `.fontSize(signal)`),
 so a change re-emits only the bound node.
 
 ### 3.3 Persisted state (`State<T>`)
 
 A `State<T>` field is the SwiftUI-`@State`-shaped form of a persisted signal,
 **auto-wired by key**:
 
 ```java
 State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);            // key = field name "count"
 State<Integer> total = new State<>(0, "total");   // explicit store key
 count.get(); count.set(0); count.update(v -> v + 1);
 count.signal();                                   // the WritableSignal (for TextField, …)
 ```
 
 The store (`StateStore`) is untyped and platform-neutral (in-memory, Redis,
 file, SQLite, LocalStorage, NVS flash). The Java realization wires `State`
 fields via an annotation processor that generates a `<View>_StateBinder` per
 view class; connection happens when the view renders. A generated DSL in a
 language without reflection/annotation processing MUST offer the equivalent
 explicit wiring.
 
 ### 3.4 Structural reactivity (conditional rendering)
 
 The tree is normally static once mounted (["`body()` is evaluated once at
 mount"](#1-design-principles-dsl-flavored)); the **only** sanctioned way to
 change *structure* reactively is a **structural container**: a slot whose
 single child subtree is selected by a signal and **reconciled** when the
 signal changes. This is the foundation for `if`/`else`, `switch`, and
 navigation ([§4.5](#45-navigation)).
 
 | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL (current) | Rust DSL (current) | Emits |
 |----------------------------|--------------------|--------------------|-------|
 | `if cond { then } else { else }` in a result builder | `Conditional.when(Signal<Boolean>, View then, View else)` | plain `if`/`match` in `build()` | `TREE` deltas (reconcile) |
 | `switch value { case a -> v; default -> d }` | `Conditional.when(Signal<T>, Case.of(T, View)...)` + `Case.otherwise(View)` | plain `if`/`match` in `build()` | `TREE` deltas (reconcile) |
 
 **Java realization** (`com.pathland.view.Conditional`): statically importable
 lowercase factories on a final class with a private constructor, mirroring
 [`Signals`](#31-signal-surface):
 
 ```java
 import static com.pathland.view.Conditional.when;
 import static com.pathland.view.Conditional.Case;
 
 when(showLogin, LoginView.of(), HomeView.of());              // if / else
 when(mode,
     Case.of(RouteMode.HOME, HomeView.of()),
     Case.of(RouteMode.USERS, UsersView.of()),
     Case.otherwise(NotFoundView.of()));                      // switch + default
 ```
 
 The names `if`, `switch`, `case`, and `else` are Java reserved keywords, so
 `when` (Kotlin's `switch` analog, and a valid Java identifier) is the method
 name, and `Case.of(...)` / `Case.otherwise(...)` carry the branches. A boolean
 signal takes the two-branch overload (`then`, `else`); an enum/int/string
 signal takes keyed `Case` branches typed to the signal's value type, with an
 optional `Case.otherwise` default.
 
 **Emission contract** (the body-once exception, formalized):
 
 1. A structural container holds a **stable slot node** (a `Group`, see
    [§8](#8-java-dsl-convergence-adopted)) whose single child is the currently
    selected content. Selection is a **content function** over the selector
    signal — `if`/`else` and `switch` are sugar over it, so value-parametrized
    content (e.g. a route param) is a first-class case.
 2. On selector change the container re-evaluates the content function,
    **renders the new subtree**, and the emitter **reconciles** it against the
    retained snapshot — emitting only `TREE` deltas (`CREATE_NODE` /
    `DELETE_NODE` / `INSERT_CHILD` / `REMOVE_CHILD` / `MOVE_CHILD`).
 3. **Identical structure emits zero opcodes.** The reconcile diffs old vs new;
    a recompute that yields the same structure produces no `TREE` deltas, so no
    equality predicate is needed on the selector signal.
 4. Structural containers **nest**: a container inside a container re-evaluates
    and reconciles its own slot independently.
 5. All other reactivity stays fine-grained (`SET_TEXT` / `SET_PROPERTY`); a
    structural container never re-emits siblings or ancestors.
 
 **Rust delta**: the Rust DSL builds `Node` trees directly and the host rebuilds
 + re-`assign_id`s + diffs on every interaction, so plain `if`/`match` in
 `build()` already produces the same reconcile — no wrapper slot and no special
 type. An optional `switch!` macro is sugar.
